newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign observers fly in as Chechens prepare to vote.
newsitem.headline: Foreign observers fly in as Chechens prepare to vote.

text.p: Several dozen foreign election observers flew in to Chechnya on Saturday, dismissing fears for their safety as the turbulent region prepared to go to the polls on Monday in a show of independence from Russia.

Chechen officials, keen to demonstrate they can keep their own house in order after Russian troops finally pulled out last month, have promised armed escorts to monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"I think the security arrangements are very, very well thought through," one Swedish observer told Reuters on arrival at Grozny airport. "I don't think there is very much risk."

Over 100 observers, including some Russians, will monitor presidential and parliamentary voting across the region of one million. About half the size of Belgium, Chechnya is sandwiched between Russia's southern plain and the soaring Caucasus Ridge.

Chechen officials have accused Russian special forces of trying to destabilise the region and undermine the legitimacy of the elections by staging attacks on foreigners and ethnic Russians. Six foreign Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds last month. Moscow hotly denies any involvement.

Despite agreeing to a peace plan following the humiliating defeat of its army by Chechnya's guerrilla forces last summer, Moscow has become increasingly irritated at the spectacle of Chechens exercising their de facto independence.
Kremlin Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin also flew in to the mainly Moslem region on Saturday for talks.
In Moscow Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin sounded a conciliatory note and said Russia would cooperate with the winner of Monday's poll.
"Let's see whom the Chechens elect as their leader. It is the will of the Chechen people and it is impermissible not to heed the will of the people," he said in a speech on Saturday.
A key element of last year's peace plan was a deal not to raise the issue of Chechen sovereignty for five years but the main candidates for the presidency all support full secession.
Russian officials have criticised the OSCE for providing some $600,000 to help the Chechens organise the elecion.
While careful not to pre-judge Monday's voting, OSCE officials are encouraged by the preparations they have seen.
For a region awash with guns after 21 months of war, the campaign, largely fought between former guerrilla leaders, has proceeded with little incident and much patriotic fervour.

As security has been stepped up, little has been seen in public of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who became separatist leader on the death of the charismatic Dzhokhar Dudayev last year, or of Aslan Maskhadov, the army commander who also made the peace.

But thousands packed Grozny's central square on Saturday to hear rival presidential candidate Shamil Basayev. A hero to the Chechens after his bloody raid against the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995, he is a wanted man in Russia but has now shed his trademark combat fatigues for a city coat and fur hat.

Moscow has also criticised Chechen authorities for failing to allow voting outside their borders, excluding hundreds of thousands of refugees who fled after President Boris Yeltsin sent in troops in December 1994 to crush a secession drive.

The quarter of a million ethnic Russians living in Chechnya before the war account for a large proportion of the refugees. Those living in nearby regions, however, will be able to vote at special polling stations set up near Chechnya's borders.

In all, 16 candidates are running for president. A key question on Monday seems likely to be whether Maskhadov, a silver-haired 45-year-old ex-colonel in the Soviet artillery, can take the 50 percent of the vote needed to win outright.
If not, he would run off in two weeks against the second candidate, most likely Yandarbiyev, Basayev or, just possibly, Movladi Udugov, the rebels' ubiquitous chief spokesman.

Many Chechens -- and Kremlin officials -- believe Maskhadov would be best able to deal with Russia, which all but encircles Chechnya and controls the supply of oil to the refineries and pipelines on which the separatists hope to rebuild prosperity.
A Moscow-backed candidate won a presidential election in December 1995, which was marked by widespread irregularities. Dudayev was also elected in an unrecognised vote in 1991.
